passages.t: ‘The LORD is my rock’, and God comes down in the storm
passages.happening:
The heading is long and gives a setting. It is a song David sang “on the day the LORD had delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul” (verse 1). It begins with love: “I love You, O LORD, my strength” (verse 1).

David piles up names for God. “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer. My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold” (verse 2).

Then he tells how near he came to death. “The cords of death encompassed me; the torrents of chaos overwhelmed me” (verse 4). He cried out, and God heard: “From His temple He heard my voice” (verse 6).

What follows is a storm. The earth shakes. Smoke and fire pour from God. “He parted the heavens and came down with dark clouds beneath His feet” (verse 9). “The LORD thundered from heaven” (verse 13).

And all that power comes down for one man. “He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters” (verse 16). “He rescued me because He delighted in me” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
This song appears twice in the Bible. It is also 2 Samuel 22, near the end of David's story, with the same heading (2 Samuel 22:1). It is a royal psalm: a king's thanksgiving after his wars.

The names for God come from David's own life. The wilderness of Judah is full of cliffs and high, hard-to-reach places. David hid in such strongholds when Saul hunted him. When he calls God ‘my rock’ and ‘my fortress’, he is thinking of the places that kept him alive. A ‘horn’ was a picture of an animal's strength, and so of power and victory.

Verses 7 to 15 describe God appearing in power, the way he came to Mount Sinai, where “there was thunder and lightning” and a thick cloud (Exodus 19:16). The poet does not mean that a storm happened on the day of a battle. He is showing what the rescue was like from heaven's side. God moved earth and sky to reach him.

‘Deep waters’ in verse 16, like ‘the torrents of chaos’ in verse 4, stand for danger beyond anyone's control, and finally for death.
passages.later:
Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, praised God for raising up “a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David” (Luke 1:69). He meant the coming Messiah.

The picture of God reaching down to pull someone from deep water comes alive in the Gospels. When Peter began to sink on the lake, “Jesus reached out His hand and took hold of Peter” (Matthew 14:31).

Paul says that in Christ God's people too are rescued: God “has rescued us from the dominion of darkness” (Colossians 1:13).
passages.hard:
Does God really come down in fire and earthquake every time someone prays? The psalm is poetry. Verses 7 to 15 do not describe the weather of one day. They describe how much God cares, in the biggest pictures the poet had.

That matters for a reader whose rescue has not come yet. The psalm does not promise a storm on demand. It promises that the God who hears ‘from His temple’ is not small, and is not far.
passages.asks:
Start where David starts: ‘I love You, O LORD.’ Many prayers begin with requests. This one begins with love.

Then make your own list. What has God been to you: a rock, a shelter, a light? Name it.

And hold on to verse 19. God did not rescue David because David was useful. ‘He rescued me because He delighted in me.’

passages.t: ‘According to my righteousness’, and ‘You light my lamp’
passages.happening:
David now says why God acted. “The LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness; He has repaid me according to the cleanness of my hands” (verse 20). “For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God” (verse 21). He says it again in verse 24.

In the middle is a saying about how God meets people. “To the faithful You show Yourself faithful, to the blameless You show Yourself blameless; to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd” (verses 25-26). “For You save an afflicted people, but You humble those with haughty eyes” (verse 27).

Then the lines of trust. “For You, O LORD, light my lamp; my God lights up my darkness” (verse 28). “For in You I can charge an army, and with my God I can scale a wall” (verse 29). “As for God, His way is perfect; the word of the LORD is flawless” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
This section is built like a frame. Verses 20 and 24 say almost the same thing, and the saying of verses 25 and 26 sits in the middle. That is a common way of stressing the centre in Hebrew poetry.

‘Clean hands’ means hands that have not done violence or taken bribes. David is speaking, above all, of his years under Saul. Twice he could have killed Saul and would not (1 Samuel 24 and 26). He did not grab the throne. He waited for God to give it.

Verse 26 is surprising. God shows himself ‘shrewd’ to the crooked. The Hebrew word comes from a word for twisting. God is not crooked, but the crooked person finds God turning every trick back on him.

A lamp in a house was a small clay dish of oil with a wick. A lamp kept burning meant the household was still alive. Later the Bible uses the lamp as a picture of David's family line continuing.
passages.later:
God speaks of “a lamp” for David in Jerusalem, his royal line kept alive (1 Kings 11:36). Jesus said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

Psalm 12:6 and Proverbs 30:5 also say that God's word is ‘flawless’ (see the note on Psalm 12).

David's life also shows the limits of ‘according to my righteousness’. The same book of Samuel that keeps this song tells of his sin with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11), and the heading of Psalm 51 links that prayer of confession to it.
passages.hard:
‘I have been blameless before Him’ (verse 23). How can David say that, when the Bible tells of his adultery and the murder of Uriah?

Many readers think he is speaking of a time and a charge: his loyalty to God through the years when Saul hunted him, when he refused to kill Saul and seize the throne. Either way, he is not claiming he never sinned. The book page explains this kind of claim in ‘When a psalmist says he is innocent’. ‘Blameless’ in the Old Testament usually means whole-hearted and loyal, not sinless.

Christians also read these lines as fully true of one person only. Hebrews says Jesus was tempted “in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
passages.asks:
Verses 25 and 26 ask a searching question. How do you meet God? With honesty and loyalty, or with twisting? The psalm says God answers in kind.

When your own lamp is low, pray verse 28. It does not ask for a sun. It asks for a lamp, enough light for the next step.

passages.t: ‘Who is the Rock except our God?’, and praise among the nations
passages.happening:
The last part asks a question that answers itself. “For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?” (verse 31).

God is the one who trains the king. “He makes my feet like those of a deer and stations me upon the heights” (verse 33). “He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze” (verse 34). Then David tells of victory in hard words: “I pursued my enemies and overtook them” (verse 37). “I ground them as dust in the face of the wind” (verse 42).

The song ends in praise. “The LORD lives, and blessed be my Rock!” (verse 46). “Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name” (verse 49). Its last line looks to the future: “He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever” (verse 50).
passages.hearers:
Deer move safely on rocky heights where people fall. The king's feet are given that sure step. ‘A bow of bronze’ need not mean a metal bow. It is a picture of strength beyond ordinary strength.

The battle lines belong to the wars of an ancient king. David fought the Philistines and the nations around Israel, and the psalm speaks of those wars in the plain language of the time.

The last verse matters most. ‘His anointed’ is the king, the mashiach. ‘David and his descendants forever’ points back to God's promise that David's family would rule for ever (2 Samuel 7:16). So the song ends not with David's victories but with God's promise.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 49 in Romans to show that God always meant the nations to praise him: “Therefore I will praise You among the Gentiles; I will sing hymns to Your name” (Romans 15:9). For Paul, the voice in the psalm is finally the voice of Christ, the son of David, through whom people of every nation come to praise God.

The promise of verse 50 is taken up when the angel tells Mary that her son will receive “the throne of His father David” (Luke 1:32).
passages.hard:
How should a Christian read a king's war song: ‘I crushed them so they could not rise’ (verse 38)?

First, as history. This is the song of a real king in an age of war, and the Bible does not hide it. Second, the psalm itself puts every victory in God's hands and ends in praise among the nations, not over them. Paul takes verse 49 as the nations joining the praise.

Third, the New Testament changes how God's people fight. Paul writes, “The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world” (2 Corinthians 10:4). No reading of this psalm gives any modern nation or army the place of God's anointed king, and none makes it right to hate an enemy. Jesus said, “love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44).
passages.asks:
Verse 31 asks what you lean on. Everyone has a ‘rock’. The psalm asks whether yours will hold.

The song also ends with a long view. David's last word is not about himself but about God's promise to people not yet born. You can pray verse 50 for your children and for those after them.
